questions.question: What does a web server do when it calls 'accept' on a listening socket?
options: It closes the current connection and opens a new one
It creates a new socket dedicated to the incoming client while the original socket continues listening
It sends an HTTP response to the client immediately
It blocks all other clients until the current request is processed
questions.explanation: The accept() system call takes the next pending connection from the queue and creates a brand-new socket for that specific client. The original listening socket remains open and continues accepting new connections.

questions.question: What is routing in the context of a web server?
options: Directing network packets through routers on the internet
Matching an incoming request's method and path to the appropriate handler function
Encrypting the request using TLS before processing
Compressing the response body for faster transmission
questions.explanation: Routing is the process of examining the HTTP method (GET, POST, etc.) and URL path of an incoming request and dispatching it to the correct handler function. For example, GET /users maps to a user listing handler.

questions.question: In the thread-per-request model, what happens when a new client connection arrives?
options: The request is added to a queue and processed later
A new thread is spawned to handle that specific connection
The server pauses all other connections to handle the new one
The request is forwarded to a separate load balancer
questions.explanation: In the thread-per-request model, each incoming connection gets its own dedicated thread. This makes the programming model simple — each thread handles one request from start to finish — but thread creation overhead and memory usage become problematic at scale.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of an event-loop model over thread-per-request?
options: It processes each individual request faster
It can handle many concurrent connections with far fewer threads, reducing memory overhead
It eliminates the need for HTTP parsing
It makes requests arrive in a guaranteed order
questions.explanation: An event loop handles thousands of concurrent connections with a single (or few) threads by never blocking on I/O. Instead of dedicating a thread per connection, it uses callbacks or async/await, dramatically reducing memory usage and context-switching overhead.

questions.question: What is middleware in a web server, and how does it work?
options: Hardware that sits between the client and server
A pipeline of functions that process the request before it reaches the route handler, each able to modify, reject, or pass along the request
A database layer that caches frequently requested data
A compression algorithm applied to all HTTP responses
questions.explanation: Middleware functions form a pipeline that each request passes through before reaching the route handler. Common middleware includes authentication, logging, rate limiting, and body parsing. Each middleware can modify the request, short-circuit with an error response, or call the next middleware.

questions.question: Why does the order of middleware in the pipeline matter?
options: It doesn't — middleware is executed in parallel regardless of order
Earlier middleware runs first, so placing authentication before logging ensures unauthenticated requests are rejected before being logged in detail
Middleware must be alphabetically ordered for the framework to parse them
The order only matters for POST requests, not GET requests
questions.explanation: Middleware executes in the order it's registered. If rate limiting runs before authentication, you limit unauthenticated spam early. If authentication runs after detailed logging, you may log sensitive data from unauthorized users. Order directly impacts security and performance.

questions.question: What problem does the C10K problem describe, and which server model addresses it?
options: The challenge of storing 10,000 files; solved by distributed file systems
The challenge of handling 10,000 simultaneous connections; addressed by event-driven architectures
The challenge of processing 10,000 database queries per second; solved by indexing
The challenge of compiling 10,000 lines of code; solved by incremental compilation
questions.explanation: The C10K problem, coined by Dan Kegel in 1999, describes the difficulty of handling 10,000 concurrent connections on a single server. Thread-per-request models struggle at this scale due to memory and context-switching overhead. Event-driven architectures like epoll/kqueue and frameworks like Node.js and Nginx were designed to solve this.

questions.question: A web server using thread-per-request has 200 threads and receives 500 simultaneous requests. Each request takes 100ms to process. What is the approximate total time to serve all 500 requests?
options: 100 ms (all run in parallel)
300 ms (3 batches of ~167 requests each)
500 ms (one request per millisecond)
50,000 ms (all requests run sequentially)
questions.explanation: With 200 threads, the server processes 200 requests concurrently in the first 100ms batch. The remaining 300 requests need two more batches: 200 in the second batch, 100 in the third. Total: approximately 300ms (3 batches x 100ms each), assuming negligible overhead.

questions.question: In an event-loop server, a handler function performs a CPU-intensive calculation that takes 500ms. What happens to all other connected clients during this time?
options: They are handled by other threads in the pool
They are all blocked because the single event-loop thread is occupied with the CPU-intensive task
They automatically reconnect to a backup server
Their requests are silently dropped
questions.explanation: In a single-threaded event loop, a CPU-intensive task blocks the entire loop for its duration. No other events — including new connections, reads, or callbacks — can be processed until the computation finishes. This is why CPU-heavy work should be offloaded to worker threads or separate processes in event-loop architectures.

questions.question:
An HTTP request arrives as raw bytes: 'GET /api/users?active=true HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Authorization: Bearer abc123

'. After parsing, which components does the server extract?
options: Only the URL path '/api/users'
Method (GET), path (/api/users), query parameter (active=true), HTTP version (1.1), and headers (Host, Authorization)
The IP address of the client and the server's SSL certificate
The response status code and body content
questions.explanation: HTTP parsing extracts the method (GET), the path (/api/users), query parameters (active=true), the protocol version (HTTP/1.1), and all headers (Host and Authorization in this case). The body would follow a blank line, but GET requests typically have no body. These parsed components drive routing and middleware decisions.
